blocks.text: Dear Ms. Phillips,

This letter sets down, so that we are both working from the same page before any work begins, the terms on which Johnson, Cross and Gibbs has asked Verdant Health Advisory to review the compensation paid to your physicians, and it asks for your signature to confirm them. We have written it plainly and at some length, because an engagement of this kind touches questions your counsel will care about, and we would rather set the terms down with care than leave either of us to infer them. If anything below does not match the understanding we reached in our conversations, I would be grateful if you would tell me before you sign rather than after.

You told us, when we first spoke, that you wanted an analysis a general counsel could rely on and a set of findings that would not surprise anyone on your side later, and that is the engagement we have scoped. The paragraphs that follow set out what we will do, who will do it, what it costs, and the terms on which we do it, in that order.
Scope and Approach

The engagement is a review of the arrangements under which your physicians are paid, undertaken to test whether those arrangements sit within the range a fair-market-value analysis would support and whether they are commercially reasonable on their own terms, apart from the volume or value of any referrals. We approach that question the way your own general counsel would want it approached, which is to say from the evidence outward rather than from a conclusion backward. Nothing in our work is meant to substitute for the legal judgment your counsel will bring; we supply the analysis on which that judgment can rest.

In practice this means we begin by collecting the compensation terms as they actually operate, not merely as the written plans describe them, and we then place each arrangement against published national survey benchmarks appropriate to the specialty, the productivity, and the market in which your physicians work. Where an arrangement falls comfortably within the supportable range we will say so and show why; where it does not, we will say that too, with the same care, and we will show our working either way. A review that only confirms what its client hoped to hear is worth very little to the counsel who has to defend it, and we will not produce one.
The Team

The work will be done by a small team, which is how we prefer to run a review of this sensitivity. Daniel Alvarado, a senior consultant who spends his working life in the economics of clinical service lines, will lead the compensation analysis and reconcile the productivity and cost figures the benchmarks turn on. Patricia Moore, an analyst on our staff, will assemble the underlying compensation data and trace each figure back to its source, so that every number in the final analysis can be shown rather than merely asserted, and I will read the analysis before it leaves this firm and remain your point of contact for anything bearing on the judgment behind it.
Fees and Payment

Our fee for the review is {{fact:f:E-2021-001.fee}}, quoted as a fixed amount for the scope described above rather than as an hourly rate, because a fixed fee keeps our attention on the quality of the analysis and lets you call with a question without watching a clock. We bill the fee in equal installments across the term of the engagement, the first on commencement and the remainder monthly thereafter, and our invoices are due within thirty days of receipt. Reasonable out-of-pocket costs, should any arise and only where you have approved them in advance, are billed at cost and itemized separately.
Term and Termination

The engagement commences on {{fact:f:E-2021-001.start}} and is planned to run for approximately three months, which is the basis on which we have scoped the fee and staffed the team. Either of us may end it on thirty days' written notice; if you end it, you owe the installments that have come due and the approved costs incurred to that date, and nothing beyond them. We would end it ourselves only if the work as agreed had become work we could not perform with the independence the analysis requires, and in that event we would return any fee paid for work not yet done.
Confidentiality

A review of physician compensation is by its nature sensitive, and we treat it accordingly. We will hold your compensation data, your internal plans, and the existence and content of this engagement in confidence, using what you share with us only for the work you have retained us to do and disclosing it no further than the members of both teams who need it to get the work done. We ask the same discretion of you as to our methods and our working papers, and where a disclosure of our findings to a third party is contemplated we ask that you route it through us first, so that nothing partial or preliminary travels under our name.
Limitation of Liability

We will carry out this engagement with the care and skill customary in our profession, and we will tell you plainly what our analysis supports and, as plainly, what it does not. We do not, however, render legal opinions, and our conclusions on fair market value are analytical judgments founded on the benchmarks and data available to us rather than guarantees of how a regulator or a court would ultimately view a given arrangement. Our total liability to you under this engagement, on any theory, is limited to the fees actually paid to us for it, and neither of us is liable to the other for indirect or consequential loss; nothing in this paragraph limits liability for fraud or willful misconduct, and nothing about it is meant to.
Governing Law

This letter is the whole of the agreement between us on this engagement and takes the place of anything discussed or drafted before it. It is governed by the law of the state in which this firm maintains its principal office, and any dispute we cannot resolve between ourselves will be heard in the courts sitting there, to whose jurisdiction we each consent. Any change to these terms is effective only if it is set down in writing and signed by both of us.
Acceptance

If this letter reflects the engagement as you understand it, please countersign below and return one copy to me, and we will confirm the first working sessions with your team at {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} shortly thereafter. We are glad to be asked to do this work, and we take the trust it implies seriously. Daniel Alvarado and Patricia Moore will be in touch within the week to arrange the first session and the initial data request.
With regards,

We are underway on the physician compensation review for {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}}, which commences on {{fact:f:E-2021-001.start}}, and the short version is that the shape of the work is clear and the early weeks belong to getting the data clean before either of us reaches for a conclusion. Our client contact is Laura Phillips, the Chief Financial Officer at Johnson, Cross and Gibbs, and hers is the sign-off we route to. I have written this memo so that the two of us are pointed the same way before the work spreads out, and so that when Laura asks where we stand we can answer with one voice rather than two.

A word on how I would like us to hold this one, because the whole value of a fair-market-value review is that a general counsel can lean on it, and that only holds if every figure we put in front of the client can be traced back to where it came from. We keep what is confirmed cleanly apart from what is still open, and we resist the pull to characterize an arrangement before the benchmarks are actually in front of us. Daniel, you have done more of these than I have, and I will lean on your read of the service-line economics; where I am unsure whether something is settled, I will assume it is not and ask you rather than guess.

One wrinkle worth naming at the outset, so a quiet delay on the inventory reads as what it is: a number of the executed compensation agreements have reached us as scanned images with no searchable text behind them, which means the underlying figures have to be keyed in by hand and checked against a second reading rather than pulled straight through. It is slow rather than difficult, and I have already built the time for it into the first week, but I want you aware of it now, so that a few extra days on the clean data reads as careful transcription and nothing more.
The work, in the order we take it up

items: The compensation data first. I will assemble the arrangements as they actually operate, not only as the written plans describe them, and trace each figure back to its source, so that nothing we carry forward rests on a number we cannot show.

Benchmark selection. Daniel Alvarado will settle which national survey benchmarks fit each specialty, productivity band, and market, since the credibility of the whole review turns on choosing the comparison honestly rather than conveniently, and on choosing it before we see where an arrangement lands.

Service-line and productivity reconciliation. Together we reconcile the productivity and cost figures the benchmarks depend on, so that when we place an arrangement against its comparison we are genuinely comparing like with like.
The client channel. A simple, steady line of communication to Laura Phillips, so that Johnson, Cross and Gibbs is never learning of a question, a gap in the data, or a delay after the fact.

blocks.text: What happens first

For this coming week the order is simple, and I would rather set it down than leave it to memory. I will open the data request and get the compensation arrangements in hand, you will start a first pass at the benchmark sources so we are not waiting on that when the data lands, and I will set a short standing check-in between the two of us to keep the workstreams honest against each other as they move. The one thing I want to have finished before we sit with the client again is a clean, sourced inventory of the arrangements under review, because everything else we do stands on it, and so that is where I am putting the week.

blocks.text: Meeting Minutes: Physician Compensation Review for {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}}
Attendees

items: Daniel Alvarado, Senior Consultant, Verdant Health Advisory
Patricia Moore, Analyst, Verdant Health Advisory
Laura Phillips, Chief Financial Officer, Johnson, Cross and Gibbs

blocks.text: Purpose

The session was a working review of the compensation data assembled to date. The object was to confirm what is sourced, mark what is still open, and agree the benchmark set before any arrangement is placed against it. No conclusions on fair market value were reached or sought at this stage.
Discussion

The team confirmed the scope of the review. It covers the physician compensation arrangements now in effect, tested for consistency with fair market value and for commercial reasonableness. It does not extend to a legal opinion, which stays with the client's counsel.

Patricia Moore walked the group through the inventory of arrangements collected so far. Most of the base compensation terms are sourced and traced to the underlying plan documents. Two productivity-based components remain open, pending figures the client will supply.

Daniel Alvarado reviewed the proposed benchmark sources. The group agreed that the benchmark for each specialty must be chosen before the comparison is drawn, not after, so the choice cannot be read as fitted to a result. Laura Phillips confirmed that Johnson, Cross and Gibbs will route the two missing productivity figures by the end of the week.

Daniel Alvarado described how the benchmarks will be applied. Each arrangement is matched to a benchmark by specialty, by productivity band, and by market. Where a physician's role spans more than one specialty, the blend used will be documented before any figure is drawn.

Patricia Moore reported on data quality. A number of the executed compensation agreements were provided as scanned images with no searchable text layer. Those figures are being keyed by hand and checked against a second reading before they enter the inventory.
The group set the standard for treating a component as confirmed. A figure is confirmed only when it is traced to a source document. Until then it is held as open and kept out of any comparison.

The group discussed the difference between the written plans and the arrangements as they actually operate. Patricia Moore noted one arrangement where the two diverge. It was agreed that the review follows the arrangement as operated, and that the divergence itself is recorded as a finding.

The scope of arrangements in the review was confirmed. It includes base salary, productivity-based compensation, and any medical directorship or call pay in effect. Arrangements changed after the review's start are logged but not analyzed unless the client asks for them.
Cadence was agreed. A short internal check will run each week. The next working session with the client will follow once the inventory is complete and the benchmark set is fixed.
Timeline was reviewed against the plan. The review is in its early phase and on schedule. Nothing discussed changed the planned sequence of work.
Action Items

rows: Key and double-check the scanned executed agreements into the inventory
Complete the sourced inventory of compensation arrangements
Finalize the benchmark set by specialty and market
Route the two open productivity figures from the client side
Record the plan-versus-practice divergence as a documented finding

blocks.text: Minutes prepared by Daniel Alvarado.
Status Report: Physician Compensation Review

Prepared for the leadership of {{fact:f:E-2021-001.client}} by Patricia Moore, of Verdant Health Advisory. This report covers the engagement through the current period, at roughly its midpoint, and is meant to give you the same picture of the work that we have.
Where the review stands

The review is on plan and on budget, and the short version is that the data is now largely in hand and sound enough that we are moving from collecting it to placing it against the benchmarks. The arrangements under review have been inventoried and, with two exceptions the client is resolving, traced to their source documents, which is the footing everything after this rests on. Nothing we have seen so far has changed our sense of the timeline or the shape of the work, and where a judgment is coming, this report is where you will first see it forming. We have kept to the practice we described at the outset, which is to lead with what the evidence shows and to hold anything the evidence does not yet support, and you will find that discipline reflected in the care of the paragraphs below.
What we completed this period

The bulk of this period went into building and sourcing the inventory of physician compensation arrangements, which is less visible than the analysis to come but is the part that decides whether the analysis can be trusted at all. I assembled the arrangements as they actually operate and traced each figure back to the plan documents and pay records behind it, so that every number carried forward can be shown rather than asserted. A share of the executed agreements reached us as scanned images with no searchable text layer, so I keyed those figures in by hand and checked each against a second reading before it entered the inventory, which is slower than pulling them straight through but is the only way to be sure the numbers we carry are the ones the parties actually signed. Daniel Alvarado settled the national survey benchmarks each arrangement will be measured against, matched to specialty, productivity, and market, and he made that selection before any comparison was drawn, which is the discipline that keeps a fair-market-value review honest. Two productivity-based components remain open while the client routes the underlying figures, but neither holds up the review as a whole, and both are expected shortly.
The work ahead

The next phase turns from assembling the data to interpreting it, and it is the heavier half of the engagement. We will place each arrangement against its chosen benchmark, identify where the compensation sits within or outside the range a fair-market-value analysis would support, and look carefully at commercial reasonableness on terms apart from the volume or value of any referrals. Where the written plan and the arrangement as operated have drifted apart, we will document the divergence and treat the arrangement as it actually functions, because that is what a reviewer after the fact would do. As findings take shape we will bring them to you as findings, with the recommendations that follow labeled plainly as recommendations, so that there is never any doubt about which is which.
Budget

Against the engagement fee of {{fact:f:E-2021-001.fee}}, we are roughly half spent at the midpoint, which tracks the plan closely. The fixed fee keeps our attention on getting the analysis right rather than on the clock, and we do not anticipate coming back for more; the remaining budget covers the analytical phase, which is the heavier half by effort even though not by fee. There have been no out-of-pocket costs of note this period, and any that arise will continue to be approved in advance and itemized, so that this line never surprises you.
Risks and things we are watching

Two items are worth your attention, and neither of them is a problem today. The first is the two open productivity components: until Johnson, Cross and Gibbs routes the underlying figures, those arrangements cannot be placed against their benchmarks, and a delay there would compress the analytical phase rather than move the review's end. The second is the gap we have already seen between one written plan and the arrangement as it operates; it is exactly the kind of thing a compensation review exists to surface, and we will treat it with care and document it fully rather than characterize it before the analysis is complete.

The one thing that would help most from your side is to close out the two open productivity figures this coming week, since the analytical phase cannot begin in earnest on those arrangements until they are in hand. Daniel Alvarado and I will keep the sourced inventory current in the meantime, and we will bring you the first placement of arrangements against their benchmarks at the next review.
